A Nile cruise is the classic Egypt trip: a floating hotel between Luxor and Aswan, temples at the stops, the river doing the travelling while you sleep. But booking pages rarely explain how the shared version works: who fills the group, who guides it, and what a day on the water looks like. This guide does exactly that for Sawa's shared cruise departures. It is written by the team behind Sawa Tours (sawa.tours), the Egypt shared-departure marketplace. We have worked in Egyptian tourism since 1993, and the river between Luxor and Aswan is the stretch we know best.

How do group Nile cruises work?

A group Nile cruise works like any cruise (your cabin, meals on board and a fixed sailing schedule) with one difference that matters: the temples come with your group's guide, and on a shared departure the group is small and confirmed before anything is charged.

The standard product sails Luxor to Aswan (or the reverse) over four or five days: the East Bank's temples at the start, the West Bank's tombs, the river south through the Esna lock, the temples of Edfu and Kom Ombo on the way, and Aswan's island temple at the end. On Sawa, the group is a shared departure: travellers pooled from several selling agencies onto one sailing date, confirmed when four travellers have reserved it (the GoAhead). Reserving costs nothing until the date confirms. For the idea behind it, see what a shared departure is.

The route: Luxor to Aswan, day by day

Nile Majesty sails the classic southbound route over five days. The shape below is illustrative; the package page carries the exact itinerary.

  1. Day 1, Luxor East Bank. The great temple complexes of the East Bank, Karnak and Luxor Temple, and boarding the boat.
  2. Day 2, West Bank, then the Esna lock. The Valley of the Kings (general ticket; special tombs such as Tutankhamun's are not included), the terraced temple of Hatshepsut and the Colossi of Memnon; then the boat sails south through the Esna lock towards Edfu.
  3. Day 3, Edfu and Kom Ombo. The Temple of Horus at Edfu, one of the most complete temples in Egypt, then back on the water to Kom Ombo's double temple, dedicated to two gods at once, and on towards Aswan.
  4. Day 4, Aswan. Philae Temple on its island and the High Dam, as the itinerary lists them.
  5. Day 5, Aswan. Breakfast on board and the cruise ends in Aswan, with the train, flights or a separate tour from the same city.

The Esna lock, explained

South of Luxor, the river is held back at the barrage town of Esna, and boats pass through a lock, a chamber that lifts a southbound vessel up to the higher water upstream (and lowers a northbound one). Boats queue for their turn, so waiting time varies from under an hour to several hours depending on traffic and scheduling. It is part of the day's rhythm rather than a delay to fear: the sundeck, tea and the lock walls rising past are a Nile cruise tradition. On most southbound sailings the lock falls on the second day, between the West Bank and Edfu.

Who do you share with, and what do you share?

Your group of up to 8 sails on a shared five-star ship and does the excursions together with its guide. What you share with your group: the guide, the excursion transport at each stop and the group's pace on shore. What you share with the ship's other guests: the sailing schedule, the restaurant and the decks. What stays your own: your cabin and your sundeck chair whenever you want it.

The group is travellers from several selling agencies on one sailing date. The departure is run by one of the licensed Egyptian agencies with travellers on the date, named before the deposit is due. Among the agencies on Sawa is a founding operating partner, Capital Travel Service (licence 2179).

The price is fixed per traveller, however the group is sourced, and it does not change as the group fills. If you are travelling alone, your cabin arrangement is confirmed in the booking, so ask before you reserve.

A day on the water

Here is an illustrative mid-cruise day, the Edfu to Aswan stretch. It shows the rhythm rather than the ship's timetable; your package page and your guide give the actual plan.

  1. Breakfast on board. A new stretch of river passes the windows.
  2. Ashore at Edfu. The group transfers from the berth to the Temple of Horus, one of the best-preserved temples in Egypt, with the building's full story readable in its walls.
  3. Back aboard and sailing. The boat turns south; the sundeck, the shade and the coffee do their work.
  4. Lunch as Kom Ombo comes into view. The temple sits directly on the river bank, one of the few you can walk to from the berth.
  5. The double temple of Kom Ombo. Dedicated to Sobek and Horus at once, with a small crocodile museum beside it. The guide covers both halves; the river side is for the sunset.
  6. Evening, sailing on towards Aswan. Dinner on board.

The rhythm is the point: the river does the travelling so the days stay temple-shaped, and nobody packs a suitcase until the last morning.

Who a shared cruise suits, and who should look elsewhere

A shared cruise departure suits couples, solo travellers, groups of friends and first-timers who want the classic Luxor to Aswan route with a guide at every temple and the logistics handled: cabin, board, excursions and the sailing schedule in one booking at a per-person price.

It is harder to recommend to three kinds of travellers. If you want a whole boat to yourselves, a private charter or a dahabiya (a small traditional sailing boat) is a different product at a different price, and not what this post covers. If your itinerary is land-paced and rigid, a fixed sailing schedule will fight it. And if mobility is a concern, ask about the boat's layout before booking: gangways, steps between deck levels and cabin access vary by vessel. The honest downsides of the shared version: the sailing date is fixed, the Esna lock waits for its turn, and the pace on shore belongs to the group, not to you alone.

How to book a shared Nile cruise with Sawa

On the Nile Majesty package page, look for a forming date, one with fewer than four travellers so far, and reserve yours free, with no card. Nothing is charged before the GoAhead.

When four travellers have reserved the date, it confirms and a 25% deposit is due by payment link; the balance is due 14 days before departure. A forming date must reach four by 30 days before the sailing; if it does not, it is cancelled, nothing is charged and we suggest another date. Once confirmed, a date is not cancelled for low numbers. Cancel 30 or more days before departure and there is no charge; 29 to 15 days before, you lose half the deposit (12.5% of the price); 14 days or fewer, or a no-show, and the deposit (25%) is retained. Some components, such as flights or cabins, may become non-refundable earlier, and this is disclosed before you pay. If force majeure (riots, a revolution and similar) stops the sailing, you get a full refund. Groups never exceed eight travellers; when a date fills, a new independent departure opens.

Payment is by a secure payment link from Online Era (General Sales Agent licence 32241); charges are in euros. The full rules are in the terms and the GoAhead promise.

faq.q: How do group Nile cruises work?
faq.a: You book a cabin on a fixed sailing with meals on board, and your group of up to 8 does the excursions together with its guide. On a shared departure, the travellers come from several selling agencies pooled onto one date. The date confirms at four travellers; nothing is charged before that, and the operating agency is named before your deposit is due.

faq.q: How many people are in a shared Nile cruise group?
faq.a: The Sawa group is four to eight travellers, confirmed at four. The ship itself carries other guests too: your group shares a five-star ship and does its excursions together with its guide.

faq.q: What does the Nile Majesty price include?
faq.a: As listed in November 2026: a five-star cruiser on full board, entrance tickets and a carriage ride, with the guided excursions in the itinerary. International flights, insurance, drinks, a balloon flight and tips are not included. Read exactly where the inclusions end on the package page before you book.

faq.q: How long does the Esna lock take?
faq.a: It varies: boats queue for their turn in the chamber, and the passage can take from under an hour to several hours depending on traffic. Most southbound sailings pass it on the second day. It is part of the river's rhythm rather than a delay to plan around.

faq.q: Is a Nile cruise good for solo travellers?
faq.a: Yes. The price is fixed per traveller, and the group gives you company at dinner, on the sundeck and at every temple. Your cabin arrangement as a solo traveller is confirmed in the booking, so ask before you reserve. The WhatsApp line (+20 109 284 7613) is answered 24/7 while your tour is running.

faq.q: Can I visit Abu Simbel from the cruise?
faq.a: Not as part of Nile Majesty. Our separate Aswan to Abu Simbel day tour is booked as its own departure, with hotel pickup in Aswan and 3.5 to 4 hours each way by road (from €50 per person, as listed in November 2026). Give it a day of its own after the cruise ends, and book flights only after each date confirms.

faq.q: What if I cancel, or the date never fills?
faq.a: If the date has not reached four travellers by 30 days before the sailing, it is cancelled and you pay nothing. If you cancel 30 or more days before departure there is no charge; from 29 to 15 days you lose half the deposit; from 14 days, the deposit is retained.
